items: “Should all women with suspected macrosomia be induced?”

blocks.text: “No. Suspected macrosomia alone does not automatically mandate induction. The decision should depend on gestational age, diabetes status, estimated fetal weight, cervical status, maternal and fetal factors, and the applicable guideline.”

content_groups.group_title: Q3. What is the most important risk factor?

items: “Maternal diabetes is an important and potentially modifiable risk factor.”

content_groups.group_title: Q4. What are other risk factors?

blocks.text: “Previous macrosomia, maternal obesity, excessive gestational weight gain, post-term pregnancy, multiparity, male fetal sex and constitutional/genetic factors.”

content_groups.group_title: Q5. What is the most important intrapartum complication?

blocks.text: Shoulder dystocia.

content_groups.group_title: Q6. What complications can shoulder dystocia cause?

blocks.text: “Brachial plexus injury, clavicular or humeral fracture, birth asphyxia and, rarely, neonatal death.”

content_groups.group_title: Q7. What maternal complications can occur?

blocks.text: “Prolonged labour, operative delivery, Caesarean delivery, severe perineal trauma and postpartum haemorrhage.”

content_groups.group_title: Q8. How do you diagnose macrosomia antenatally?

blocks.text: “It is suspected clinically from excessive fundal height and assessed using ultrasound fetal biometry, particularly estimated fetal weight and abdominal circumference, recognising that ultrasound estimation has significant limitations.”

content_groups.group_title: Q9. How accurate is ultrasound EFW?

blocks.text: “It is an estimate rather than a direct measurement. Errors of approximately 8–15% have been reported, with poorer accuracy at the extremes of fetal weight and in diabetes.” NICE

content_groups.group_title: Q10. Does macrosomia mean Caesarean section?

blocks.text: “No. The decision is individualised according to estimated fetal weight, diabetes status, previous obstetric history and other maternal and fetal factors.”
“Not automatically. Suspected macrosomia alone does not necessarily require induction; management depends on the clinical circumstances and applicable guideline.”

content_groups.group_title: Q12. Can a 3.5 kg baby cause shoulder dystocia?

blocks.text: Yes.
This is an important point.
“Shoulder dystocia is difficult to predict and can occur even when the fetus is not macrosomic.”

content_groups.group_title: Q13. Why does diabetes cause macrosomia?

blocks.text: Insulin is a fetal growth-promoting hormone.
Maternal hyperglycaemia → increased glucose transfer to fetus → fetal hyperglycaemia → fetal hyperinsulinaemia → increased growth and fat deposition.
This particularly contributes to increased:
Abdominal circumference and fetal adiposity.

When you see:
Think:
1. DATES Confirm gestational age.
2. DIABETES Screen/assess glycaemic control.
3. DEVELOPMENT Assess fetal growth, EFW, AC, liquor and wellbeing.
4. DELIVERY Discuss timing and mode of delivery based on risk.
If the examiner asks:
Say:

“I would first confirm the gestational age and review previous fetal growth. I would assess maternal risk factors, particularly diabetes, obesity, excessive weight gain and previous macrosomia or shoulder dystocia. I would perform an obstetric examination and ultrasound assessment of fetal biometry, particularly estimated fetal weight and abdominal circumference, while recognising the limitations of ultrasound estimation. I would assess amniotic fluid and fetal wellbeing as clinically indicated. I would optimise maternal diabetes where present and discuss the risks of shoulder dystocia, birth trauma, operative delivery and postpartum haemorrhage. Finally, I would individualise the timing and mode of delivery according to the estimated fetal weight, diabetes status, previous obstetric history, gestational age, maternal and fetal factors and local guidelines.”
